chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Abdullah ibn Ahmad al-Razi, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Isma'il ibn Mihran, from Muhammad ibn Hafs, from Yaqoob ibn Bashir, from Jabir, from Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

A man went to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) in Basra and said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, inform us about brothers.' He replied, 'Brothers are of two types: brothers of trust and brothers of companionship. As for brothers of trust, they are like your hand, wing, family, and wealth. When you find a brother at the level of trust, expend your wealth and body for him, befriend his friends, and be an enemy of his enemies. Conceal his secret and flaw, and manifest his good qualities. And know, O questioner, that they are fewer than red sulfur. As for brothers of companionship, you derive pleasure from them, so do not cut off that pleasure from them, and do not seek beyond that what is in their inner selves, and expend for them what they expended for you in terms of pleasant countenance and sweet speech.'

key_terms.الكبريت الأحمر: Red sulfur (used as a metaphor for scarcity)

ai.seo_question: What are the two types of friends in Shia Islam and how should one treat them?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq attributes this nuanced classification of friendship to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), reflecting the Shia emphasis on *wilayah* and social hierarchy. The 'brothers of trust' represent the elite few who warrant total self-sacrifice and secrecy, echoing the rarity of true *kufu* (compatibility) in spiritual bonds, while 'brothers of companionship' denote a pragmatic, pleasurable social tier where one avoids probing inner secrets (*ضمير*). This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly view on balancing deep spiritual loyalty with practical social etiquette.
